Killer
KIL-er
adjective (Gen X slang)
From kill + -er, one who kills. The inverted sense, "excellent, formidable," goes back to 1930s swing-era jive (killer-diller, a sensational tune or performer) and to the show-business boast that a comic "killed" an audience. Gen X made it a stock adjective in 1980s surf, skate, and teen speech — killer waves, a killer party, killer as a one-word verdict — and the computer trade coined killer app by the late 1980s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In Gen X speech killer was praise: a killer wave, a killer guitar solo, a killer deal. "How was the concert?" "Killer." The word works the way bad and wicked work in slang — by flipping a dark word into a compliment. The Christian observation is not that a teenager who says killer is bloodthirsty; it is that a culture which makes death its highest compliment has grown careless about death. God has not. "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13) guards the image of God in every man. Our Lord named the first killer plainly: the devil "was a murderer from the beginning" (Joh 8:44), and he still comes "to steal, and to kill, and to destroy" (Joh 10:10). The gospel then tells the darkest use of the word in history: men "killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead" (Act 3:15). The world’s worst killing became the world’s life, because Christ came "that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly" (Joh 10:10). Words shape what we laugh at and what we admire: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Pro 18:21). A father need not police every killer his son says about a skateboard trick; but he can teach him that the word was borrowed from the enemy’s trade, and that the most excellent thing in the world is not a killer but a Life-giver.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X surf, skate, and teen slang (1980s; from 1930s jive killer-diller) for excellent, formidable; a death-word turned compliment, set against the Life-giver who came that we might have life (Joh 10:10).

KILLER, adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s, surf, skate, and teen speech) Excellent, formidable, outstanding. "Killer waves at the point today." "That solo was killer."

Antecedents: 1930s swing-era killer-diller; show-business "he killed" (was a hit). Compounds: killer app (late 1980s), killer deal.

Kin to the inversion slang of bad, wicked, and later sick: a dark word flipped into praise.

Webster 1828: KILLER, n. One who deprives of life; he or that which kills.

Decode for parents: "killer" just means great; but teach why death-words became compliments, and Who actually gives life.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:13 — "Thou shalt not kill."

Joh 8:44 — "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it."

Joh 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

Act 3:15 — "And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses."

Pro 18:21 — "Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof."

Modern Corruption

Killer turns the devil’s trade into a compliment; Scripture names the murderer from the beginning and crowns instead the Prince of life, whom men killed and God raised.

expand to see more

The inversion habit. Bad, wicked, killer, and later sick share a pattern: the darker the word, the higher the praise. Part of this is simple youthful exaggeration; part of it is a culture that finds evil more interesting than good and death more thrilling than life. Isaiah pronounced woe on those "that call evil good, and good evil" (Isa 5:20). Slang inversion is not the same sin, but it trains the ear in the same direction, and a family does well to notice it.

The Prince of life. The deepest answer to killer is Peter’s sermon in Solomon’s porch: they "killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead" (Act 3:15). The devil is the true killer (Joh 8:44); Christ is the true life (Joh 10:10). A Christian can still call a wave killer, but he knows that death is an enemy, not a compliment, and that the last enemy has been defeated by an empty tomb.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English killen (to strike, slay) → killer (one who kills) → 1930s jive killer-diller → 1980s surf and teen killer (excellent); Scripture: the Prince of life (Act 3:15).

expand to see more

Middle English killen — to strike, to slay; killer — one who kills

Show-business "to kill" an audience — to be a smash hit

1930s swing jive: killer-diller — a sensational tune or performer

1980s surf, skate, and teen speech: killer — excellent; late-1980s killer app

Biblical counterword: the murderer from the beginning (Joh 8:44) vs. the Prince of life (Act 3:15)

Usage

""Dude, that was a killer ollie.""

"The thief cometh … to kill; Christ came that we might have life (Joh 10:10)."

"Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21)."
